history_of_present_illness: Hookworm disease can present insidiously, often leading to a severe and fatal anemia. Early symptoms may include a dermatitis, often called "ground itch" or "foot itch," at the site of larval penetration, which typically disappears in about two weeks unless secondary infection occurs. Pulmonary irritation, such as cough and bronchitis, may occur during larval migration through the lungs. Marked cases often show pronounced anaemia with a yellow, wax-like skin, epigastric tenderness with frequent acid eructations, cardiac palpitation, shortness of breath on exertion, headache, and vertigo. Severe cases can lead to extreme anaemia (Hb as low as 15%), marked weakness, dyspnoea, stomach dilatation, protuberant abdomen, oedema (especially of feet and ankles), tinnitus aurium, and depravity of appetite (e.g., dirt eating). In children, the disease causes marked stunting of physical growth and mental backwardness, with striking lack of sexual development (delayed or absent menstruation, absence of pubic hair). The skin is often dry and of a pale earthy or tallow-yellow color, especially on the alae of the nose and forehead. Eye characteristics may resemble those of a fish or intoxicated person, with a tendency for pupils to dilate in bright light, and in severe cases, retinal hemorrhages and night blindness may occur. Ascites can be present in advanced cases.
exposure_and_epidemiology: Hookworm disease is caused primarily by two parasites: *Ancylostoma duodenale* (Old World species) and *Necator americanus* (New World species), both belonging to the class Nematoda and family Strongylidae. A new species, *A. ceylanicum*, has also been reported in man. The disease is rare outside tropical and subtropical countries, except in mines or tunnels with suitable warmth and moisture. It is highly prevalent in India, Egypt, China, other parts of the East, Porto Rico, Philippine Islands, South America (especially Brazil), Central America, Mexico, the Southern States of the U.S., and many Pacific islands. It is also common in southern Europe. The infection occurs when infective larvae, which develop from eggs passed in human faeces, penetrate the skin, usually through bare feet, or less commonly, are ingested. The eggs develop into rhabditiform larvae in one to two days in conditions of moisture, warmth, and shade (optimal temperature around 27°C, no development beyond 37°C or below 14°C). These larvae molt, retaining a protective sheath, becoming non-feeding, motile, and infective strongyloid larvae that can live for months in moist, shaded soil but are rapidly killed by drying or sunlight. Porous, sandy soil is more favorable for larval development than clay. Lack of proper sewage systems and open-air defecation contribute significantly to soil infestation. Infected mines with temperatures above 25°C show high infection rates (61%). Individuals of the negro race appear to have some immunity compared to whites but can serve as carriers. Parasites can live in man for several months to two or three years, with some cases clearing within seven years without re-infection.
vitals: Pulse rate averages about 110, and blood pressure is low in marked cases. Temperature is usually normal in uncomplicated cases, though pulmonary manifestations may occur during larval migration in the first week or so following heavy infection.
physical_exam: Physical examination may reveal a dermatitis at the site of larval penetration (often feet or toes), sometimes with vesicles that can become pustular or impetiginous due to scratching. In severe cases, there is pronounced anaemia with yellow, wax-like skin, but emaciation is rare as subcutaneous fat remains. Oedema is frequently observed, especially around the ankles and feet. The jejunum may show small hemorrhagic spots, sometimes with a worm at the center. The heart often shows fatty degeneration and dilatation, with functional murmurs and pulsation of neck veins in advanced stages; right-side cardiac dilatation and high pulse pressure are common in severe cases. Liver and kidneys usually show fatty changes, while the spleen is generally shrunken (though some reports note enlargement). The skin is typically very dry, pale earthy, or tallow-yellow, particularly on the alae of the nose and forehead. Hair may be dry and scanty or absent in pubic and beard regions. Patients may appear pot-bellied, and stomach dilatation is common. Eye characteristics can be fish-like or intoxicated-appearing, with pupil dilation instead of contraction to bright light; retinal hemorrhages and night blindness can occur in severe cases. Children show marked stunting of growth, mental backwardness, and lack of sexual development. Ascites may be present in advanced cases.
labs_and_diagnostics: Laboratory diagnosis almost invariably involves finding hookworm ova in the faeces. The eggs are oval, thin-shelled, with a wide, clear, glassy zone separating the segmented, granular central portion from the shell. In freshly passed faeces, ova show only commencing segmentation (rarely more than 4 or 8 segments), as anaerobic conditions in the intestines prevent full embryonic development. In contrast, *Strongyloides* larvae are typically found actively moving in fresh faeces, or eggs contain fully developed embryos. The rhabditiform hookworm embryo is 200 × 14 microns, with a mouth cavity as deep as the embryo's diameter at its posterior end (compared to *Strongyloides*'s half as deep). The genital anlage of *Strongyloides* is also much larger. Microscopic examination of fresh faecal smears (e.g., with water or 1% trikresol solution) or cultural methods can identify larvae. Concentration techniques like Bass's method (centrifugation with calcium chloride solutions of specific gravities 1.050 and 1.250 to float eggs) or Barber's technique (emulsifying faeces in glycerine and saturated salt solution to float eggs) are useful. Lane's levitation method involves mixing sediment with water on a slide, allowing it to stand, then immersing in water; ova stick to the slide and are concentrated ten-fold. Diagnosis can also be made by finding worms in the stool after thymol treatment. A phenolphthalein test for occult blood can indicate mucosal lesions. Blood tests in marked cases show red cell counts averaging 2,500,000 to 3,000,000 per cu. mm., and Hb percentages between 30 and 50. The color index is typically well below 1, but in rare cases, it can be above 1 (pernicious anaemia-like). A moderate leucocytosis may occur, but white count is usually normal. Eosinophilia (15-35% of leukocytes) is characteristic, but tends to disappear in advanced cases. Charcot-Leyden crystals are often present in stools. Albuminuria is common in advanced cases with oedema, but casts are rare.
differential_diagnosis: Beriberi, chronic nephritis, and malarial cachexia. Heavy *Ascaris* infections can also cause similar symptoms. Differential points include: multiple neuritis signs for beriberi, presence of casts or high blood pressure for chronic nephritis, and typically no splenic enlargement in ancylostomiasis (differentiating it from malaria and kala-azar).
management_and_clinical_course: The prognosis is generally good with treatment, but is more serious in children due to interference with physical and mental development. The disease tends to shorten life and increases susceptibility to intercurrent diseases, with mortality ranging from less than 0.5% to 7%. The presence of eosinophilia indicates a good prognosis, while its absence suggests hematopoietic system exhaustion. Prophylaxis focuses on diagnosing and treating carriers, proper disposal of faecal material (burning, boiling, septic tanks, or burial away from water supplies), and preventing soil pollution. The use of properly constructed privies and wearing shoes are crucial. Treatment involves anthelmintic drugs. Thymol (introduced in 1879) is given in divided doses (e.g., 60 grains total for adults) in capsules or cachets, preferably triturated with sugar of milk. Patients must avoid fats and alcohol during treatment due to the risk of poisoning. Epsom salts are used as a purgative before and after the thymol doses. Side effects can include burning in the stomach, tingling, cardiac weakness, and respiratory distress, treated with coffee, strychnine, or aromatic spirits of ammonia. Carbon tetrachloride is highly promising, being cheaper, more effective, and safer than thymol or chenopodium when chemically pure. A dose of 3 cc in hard gelatin capsules is effective against hookworms and ascarids, and larger doses up to 10-12 cc have been safely employed; it does not require purgatives. Oil of chenopodium is another effective treatment; a recommended dose is 1.5 cc in three divided doses (0.5 cc each). Deaths have occurred with doses of 2-3 cc, so lower doses are preferred. Side effects include dizziness, depression, unsteady gait, partial loss of consciousness, tingling, and epigastric burning. Castor oil is important for chenopodium poisoning. Beta-naphthol (e.g., 60 grains) is effective but is a renal irritant. Combination with phenolphthalein (5 grains beta-naphthol + 1 grain phenolphthalein) can eliminate the need for purgation. After expelling worms, iron or arsenic tonics are advised, with arsenic preferred for pernicious anaemia-like tendencies. Ground itch is treated with zinc oxide ointment with 10 grains salicylic acid per ounce, or 3% salicylic acid in alcohol.
